sections.title: Get the band right: South Africa's dual UHF allocation (915.4-919 MHz + 865.6-867.6 MHz)
sections.intro: The single most expensive mistake in cross-border RFID sourcing is a band-and-reader mismatch — our [RFID frequency guide](/blog/rfid-frequencies-lf-hf-uhf-explained/) covers the LF/HF/UHF split and the [read-range guide](/blog/how-far-uhf-rfid-tag-read/) shows what a mismatch costs. South Africa is unusual: ICASA permits two UHF RFID bands, so "get the band right" means matching the inlay to the readers you run, not to a single national frequency. The high-power option is 915.4-919 MHz at 4 W EIRP with frequency hopping — it sits inside the upper US 902-928 MHz band, just below Australia's 920-926 MHz, and nowhere near the EU 865-868 MHz band. There is also an EU-harmonised sub-band at 865.6-867.6 MHz (2 W ERP) and a 919.2-921 MHz allocation for non-modulating devices.

sections.title: Landed cost: HS 8523.52, MFN import duty and 15% VAT
sections.intro: The unit price is the headline; the landed cost is the story. For South Africa there are three characters — the HS line, the general (MFN) import duty with no China-South Africa preference, and the 15% VAT.

dataHighlight.heading: South Africa charges 15% VAT on the added-tax value — plus duty by tariff
dataHighlight.text: RFID cards and inlays classify under HS 8523.52 ("smart cards"). Unlike Australia's ChAFTA, there is no China-South Africa free trade agreement that lowers South African import duty on Chinese-origin goods, so the general (MFN) rate in the SARS tariff schedule applies — for many electronics that rate is low, but the exact line must be confirmed with your broker. On top of any duty, South Africa levies 15% VAT, charged on the added-tax value: the customs value uplifted by 10% (the standard uplift on non-SACU-origin imports) plus duty. VAT is generally claimable as input tax by a VAT-registered importer. On a DDP quote, freight, duty, the 15% VAT and clearance are all included in the price you see — no border surprises. Confirm the exact tariff line and any rebates with your customs broker.

faq.question: Which UHF band do your tags use for South Africa?
faq.answer: South Africa is a dual-band RAIN market under ICASA. The high-power band is 915.4-919 MHz at up to 4 W EIRP with frequency hopping; there is also an EU-harmonised sub-band at 865.6-867.6 MHz (2 W ERP) and a 919.2-921 MHz allocation for non-modulating devices. Because both bands are legal, we tune inlays to match the readers you run rather than a single national frequency — the 915.4-919 MHz band suits most warehouse and asset deployments. HF access-control cards at 13.56 MHz are globally harmonised and unaffected, so specify the UHF band only for inlay and label orders.

faq.question: Are your RFID cards compatible with Impro, Gallagher and HID access control systems?
faq.answer: Yes. Impro, Gallagher, HID and other systems support standard ISO 14443A MIFARE cards and 125 kHz proximity cards. Our MIFARE Classic 1K and EM4100 cards are manufactured to these exact international standards, and DESFire EV3 (AES-128) is available for high-security sites. Because reader configurations vary, we ship free sample cards to your South African address so you can confirm compatibility on your live readers before any bulk order.

faq.question: Do RFID products need ICASA type approval and an NRCS Letter of Authority to import into South Africa?
faq.answer: Radio equipment — readers and interrogators — must be ICASA type-approved before it is imported or sold, and powered electrical/electronic apparatus needs an NRCS Letter of Authority (LOA); SARS will not clear regulated goods without a valid LOA. Passive RFID tags, inlays and cards are field devices rather than marked radio equipment. ICASA type approval is issued to a South-African-registered entity, so approvals typically sit with the reader vendor or your local integrator — we supply the conformance documentation (ISO 14443 / ISO/IEC 18000-63) to support it.

faq.question: How do South African VAT and import duties work on an order?
faq.answer: RFID smart cards classify under HS 8523.52. There is no China-South Africa free trade agreement that lowers South African import duty on Chinese-origin goods, so the general (MFN) rate in the SARS tariff schedule applies — many electronics carry a low rate, but confirm the exact line with your broker. South Africa then levies 15% VAT on the added-tax value (customs value + 10% uplift on non-SACU-origin goods + duty), generally claimable as input tax by a VAT-registered importer. On a DDP quote, freight, duty, the 15% VAT and clearance are included in the price up front.

faq.question: What is the total delivery time to South Africa including production?
faq.answer: A typical first order runs about 10-15 business days end to end: samples in the first few days, 3-10 days production and read-testing, then 5-8 business days express air to OR Tambo (Johannesburg), Cape Town, King Shaka (Durban) or Pretoria. Bulk programmes on sea freight take roughly 18-25 days in transit and are planned against a blanket agreement.

faq.question: Can I get samples before placing a large order, and what is the MOQ?
faq.answer: Yes — free sample kits ship to South African addresses so you can test read performance and reader compatibility on your own hardware first, and for UHF orders the samples are tuned to your chosen South African band so the test reflects field conditions. MOQ depends on the product and personalisation and is quoted per order with your target card or inlay, artwork and annual volume.
